---
title: "PowerPoint decks"
jupyter: python3
---

```{python}
import ezrsurvey as ez
```

The deck is where a survey project ends, and rebuilding it by hand every wave is
where the time goes. Two routes are provided: one call for a deck with no
particular shape, and a slide-at-a-time builder for a deck that has one. Both
write a real `.pptx` through `python-pptx`, so the result opens in PowerPoint,
Keynote and Google Slides. They need the `reports` extra:

```bash
pip install "ezrsurvey[reports]"
```

Everything below writes into a temporary folder. In your own work a bare file
name lands in `ezrsurvey-outputs/`.

```{python}
import os
import tempfile

deck_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
```

## One call

Give `report_deck()` a dict. The keys become slide titles, and each value
becomes the slide's content.

```{python}
ez.report_deck(
    {
        "Who follows pod racing?": ez.plot_bars(ez.calc_percentage(ez.podracing_survey, "demo_gender")),
        "How likely are they to recommend it?": ez.calc_nps(ez.podracing_survey, "nps_value"),
    },
    path=os.path.join(deck_dir, "overview.pptx"),
    title="Pod-Racing Fan Survey",
)
```

The content is handled according to what it is. A chart becomes an image sized
to the layout's content placeholder, a data frame becomes a table sized to fill
the slide, and a list of strings becomes a bullet list.

## A slide at a time

A deck with chapters, dividers and commentary is assembled step by step. Each
call takes the document and returns it, so the deck is built by passing it from
one call to the next.

```{python}
drivers = ez.ipm_model(ez.podracing_survey, "nps_value", "ratings_")

deck = ez.report_new("pptx")
deck = ez.report_title_slide(deck, "Pod-Racing Fan Survey", subtitle="1,000 fans | Fieldwork 2026")
deck = ez.report_section(deck, "RECOMMENDATION")
deck = ez.report_slide(
    deck,
    "How likely are you to recommend pod racing?",
    ez.plot_nps(ez.podracing_survey, "nps_value"),
)
deck = ez.report_section(deck, "RATINGS")
deck = ez.report_slide(deck, "Which aspects matter most, and which fall short?", ez.plot_ipm(drivers))
deck = ez.report_add_slide(deck, "What we should fix first")
deck = ez.report_add_text(deck, [
    "Value and commentary sit lowest and matter most.",
    "Atmosphere is already strong; further gains there move nothing.",
])
ez.report_save(deck, os.path.join(deck_dir, "deck.pptx"))
```

`report_slide()` is title plus one thing, which is most slides.
`report_add_slide()` opens a slide you then add to with `report_add_plot()`,
`report_add_table()` and `report_add_text()`, for the slides that carry more than
one element.

The same calls produce a Word document. Sections become headings rather than
dividers:

```{python}
doc = ez.report_new("docx")
doc = ez.report_section(doc, "Pod-Racing Fan Survey")
doc = ez.report_add_text(doc, "Net Promoter Score and the drivers behind it.")
doc = ez.report_add_table(doc, drivers)
ez.report_save(doc, os.path.join(deck_dir, "report.docx"))
```

## Your organisation's template

Point ezrsurvey at a template once and everything downstream matches it:

```python
ez.use_brand("brand/org-template.pptx")
```

That reads the template's theme: accent colours become the palette behind
`plot_bars()`, `pal_brand()` and `scale_fill_brand()`, the body typeface becomes
the default for `theme_ezrsurvey()`, and the file itself becomes the reference
document for `report_new()`, `report_deck()` and `scaffold_report()`. With no
template to hand, set the values directly:

```{python}
ez.use_brand(colors=["#0B5394", "#E69138"], fonts="Georgia", quiet=True)
palette = ez.pal_brand()
ez.clear_brand()
palette
```

Both live in an `.ezrsurvey.yml` profile if you want them for every project. The
profile is the same file the R package reads, so a team working in both
languages shares one. The semantic palettes keep their meaning whatever the
brand: `pal_rating` and `pal_nps` stay red-amber-green, because recolouring a
detractor to match a logo would make the chart lie.

> A brand typeface only reaches the chart when it is installed on the machine
> drawing it. If it is not, charts fall back to the default sans-serif and
> ezrsurvey says so once, naming the font.

Layouts are chosen by inspecting a template's placeholders rather than their
names, so a template written in any language works. `report_layouts()` shows
what yours offers:

```{python}
ez.report_layouts()
```

## Without a template

Decks default to the package's own 16:9 template: a full-bleed cover with a
large title and a subtitle strapline, full-bleed section dividers, and content
slides carrying a left-aligned title over a slim rule with a live slide number
in the corner.

```python
ez.report_deck(items, path="deck.pptx")                   # styled, the default
ez.report_deck(items, path="deck.pptx", style="plain")    # same palette, no decoration
ez.report_new("pptx", slide_numbers=False)                # drop the numbering
```

Charts are drawn at a constant bar thickness whatever the answer count, so a
three-answer chart and a ten-answer chart sit together in a deck instead of the
first one's bars turning into slabs. `bar_width` and `bar_ref_items` in
`ezrsurvey_options()` control it.

## Google Slides

Google Slides imports PowerPoint natively, so the route above is also the Google
Slides route: build the deck, then use **File > Import slides**, or open the
`.pptx` straight from Drive.

Chart images, text boxes, bullets, speaker notes and theme colours all survive
the import. Two things to watch. Fonts outside Google's catalogue are
substituted, so if Slides is the destination, brand with one that is in it
(`ez.use_brand(..., fonts="Roboto")`). And intricate table borders simplify.
Charts are saved as transparent-background PNGs, so they sit cleanly on any
Slides background.
